one_liner: The Odin compiler at its default -o:minimal builds a 40,000-procedure generated file 1.3-2.7x faster than GCC compiles the C twin, but slower than clang.
what_it_does: Odin is a general-purpose, data-oriented systems language ('The Data-Oriented Language for Sane Software Development') with its own C++ compiler that type-checks packages and generates native code through LLVM; on Linux it links through the clang driver. It is not a drop-in for gcc: it compiles Odin source, not C. This entry is about how long an unoptimised build takes, not about the speed of the generated code.
how_it_is_fast: Not the front end: Odin's check alone costs 19.1 us/f against 11.9 for gcc -fsyntax-only and 13.5 for clang. The gain over GCC is in code generation: Odin's whole build minus its check is about 128 us/f (including the lld link and compiling its own runtime and core:os packages), while GCC's object-only -O0 path costs 182 us/f (gcc 15) to 388 us/f (gcc 16) beyond its syntax check (derived from page data). Odin's default -o:minimal runs a short LLVM IR pipeline (SROA, early-CSE, instsimplify, simplifycfg, always-inline per src/llvm_backend_passes.cpp) and then LLVM code generation at CodeGenLevelNone (src/llvm_backend.cpp), emitting several build units that are linked together (the -use-separate-modules default at that level, per the compiler's help text). In effect Odin inherits LLVM's fast no-optimisation backend, the same one that puts clang ahead of gcc in this table, and adds a heavier front end, so it lands between clang and gcc; the suite itself names no mechanism.
when_to_use: Debug-build turnaround for Odin projects when the alternative on the table is C or C++ built with GCC: a full Odin build of plain procedures ran 1.3x faster than gcc 15's object-only -c and 2.7x faster than gcc 16.2.1's (derived from page data).

Generic code: Odin's parametric-polymorphic variant built in 98 us/f, against 600 and 566 us/f for g++ 15 and 16 templates and 107 for clang++, and far below C3 (255) and rustc (238) in the same table.

Hosts where the compiler may use every core: Odin starts one worker thread per online CPU by default, which this benchmark disabled by pinning each compiler to one core (inference: unpinned speed was not measured).
Compact debug-level binaries: 112.6 B per function against 121.1 for gcc and 146.1 for clang, because -o:minimal already runs SROA and CSE.
when_not_to_use: If you could compile C with clang: clang 23.1.1 built the C version faster (link-free Compile 77.9 us/f, Total 118 vs Odin's 147), and clang++ compiled the untemplated C++ in 82.4.
If compile speed is the main reason to switch: dmd (13 us/f), Zig (110), Free Pascal (138) and the single-pass C compilers tcc (4), cuik (76) and cproc (86) built the same program faster.

Memory-limited build machines: Odin's build peaked at 34.0 kB per function (sampled RSS summed over the compiler's process tree), about 1.36 GB for the 40,000-procedure file, against 17.2 kB/f for gcc 15 (about 0.69 GB) and 6.8 kB/f for clang (about 0.27 GB), so 2-5x more (derived from page data).

Optimised release builds: the benchmark ran only Odin's default -o:minimal and gcc/clang at default -O0, so it says nothing about -o:speed build times (single build unit, LLVM default code generation) or run-time speed.

WSL2 or other virtualised Linux hosts: open issue #7128 shows the default thread pool thrashing on futexes (a hello-world build took 2381 ms, 767 ms with -thread-count:1); the README also warns that the compiler is still in development.

integration.form: compiler toolchain (command-line compiler; release and nightly builds linked from the README, or build from source)
integration.dependencies: LLVM as the backend; on Linux the clang driver for linking (src/linker.cpp runs `clang`, overridable with ODIN_CLANG_PATH) plus lld when -linker:lld is passed, as in this benchmark
integration.min_toolchain: odin dev-2026-09:a2fb372b7 as measured (monthly dev tag)
integration.platforms: Windows, Linux and macOS per the README badge; measured on x86-64 Arch Linux only
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (command-line compiler); defaults to one worker thread per online CPU (gb_affinity_init uses sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN) and ignores the affinity mask), override with -thread-count

gotchas: Harness asymmetry and noisy Total cells: Odin links with clang -fuse-ld=lld (-linker:lld) while gcc and g++ use the default system linker, and the harness runs no link-free compile step for Odin. The Total column behind the record's 2.7x over gcc 15 is unstable (gcc 15's C Total of 392 is double its own Compile of 193.8; clang++'s templated Total of 107 is below its Compile of 128.7). A conservative reading puts Odin's whole build, link included (147 us/f), against GCC's object-only -c: still 1.3x faster than gcc 15 (193.8), 2.7x than gcc 16.2.1 (400.1), 1.8x than g++ 15 (269.6) and 2.5x than g++ 16.2.1 (372.3). The win over GCC survives the linker asymmetry, but the headline against gcc 15 shrinks from 2.7x to 1.3x.

Unequal work that counts against Odin: -o:minimal runs SROA, early-CSE, instsimplify and simplifycfg, more than gcc or clang do at -O0, and every Odin build type-checks and compiles base:runtime and core:os from source, because the generated program imports core:os for os.exit, while C links a precompiled libc. The C side adds only -Wall -Wextra.

Concurrency and pinning: tasks run at the same time in a multiprocessing pool with each worker pinned to one CPU by os.sched_setaffinity. Odin ignores that mask and starts one thread per online CPU, so all of them time-share one core (issue #7128 shows how costly its futex-based pool can be on some hosts). cpu_topology.py's frequency path does not drop SMT siblings, so two compilers may have shared one physical core. Odin's 5.9 s builds, like every gcc build over 3 s, keep the minimum of only 2 repetitions.

Unexplained cells and unchecked output: Odin's templated build (98) is faster than its untemplated one (147) even though its templated check is 2.5x slower (47.0 vs 19.1), which implies 2.5x cheaper code generation for generic procedures; noise is the likelier explanation. The README prose figures (odin 92, clang 87 us/f) come from a different run than the tables. The harness ignores the built binary's exit code and result.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Of the nordlow/compiler-benchmark siblings, dmd (13 us/f) is more than ten times faster and Zig (110/92) is faster on both variants. C3 (153/255) roughly ties Odin on plain code but is 2.6x slower on generics, and rustc (187/238) is slower on both. Pick Odin when you want a C alternative whose default debug builds beat GCC and stay cheap with generic code, not for the fastest compiler in the table.
verified_claims_summary: One run of nordlow/compiler-benchmark (tables committed in d16d0a5 on 2026-10-09) on an AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 under Arch Linux generated 200 x 200 arithmetic call-chain procedures. odin dev-2026-09:a2fb372b7 at its default -o:minimal built the Odin version, lld link included, in 147 us per function (98 templated). For the same C at default -O0 with -Wall -Wextra, gcc 15.3.0 took 392 Total (193.8 object-only) and gcc 16.2.1 took 454 (400.1); clang 23.1.1 was faster at 118 (77.9). Odin's check step (19.1 us/f) was slower than gcc -fsyntax-only (11.9).
status_note: Odin is actively developed (12.1k stars, 20,065 commits, 770 open issues, Zlib licence, last commit 2026-10-11 per the verification record) but pre-1.0, with monthly dev tags and a README warning that the compiler is still in development; the evidence is one run on one laptop by an independent developer using a public MIT harness.
